methods.label: Count the sets of enclosed cells
methods.explanation:
Instead of choosing toothpicks one at a time, record which cells lie inside the loop. A side carries a toothpick exactly when it separates an inside cell from an outside cell, treating everything beyond the grid as outside. Thus the enclosed cells determine the toothpicks uniquely. Moreover, the enclosed cells must be connected through shared sides; a connection only at a corner would make the boundary meet itself.

Number the columns \(1\) through \(8\). Every middle-row cell has exactly one covered side. If that cell is outside, exactly one of its four neighboring positions is inside. If it is inside, exactly one neighboring position is outside.

First suppose no middle-row cell is inside. Each column must then have exactly one of its top and bottom cells inside. Since the middle row separates the top and bottom rows, connectivity forces all eight chosen cells to be in the same row. Enclosing the entire top row or the entire bottom row gives \(2\) loops.

Now suppose some middle-row cells are inside. An outside middle cell next to an inside middle cell already has its one covered side. Its top and bottom neighbors must therefore be outside, making its entire column outside. Such a column cannot separate two groups of enclosed cells. Consequently the inside middle cells form one consecutive run.

Let \(s\) and \(e\) be the first and last columns of that run. If \(s\ge3\), column \(s-1\) is entirely outside. The middle cell in column \(s-2\) has no inside middle neighbor, so its clue forces one of its top and bottom neighbors to be inside. That cell would be disconnected from the run by column \(s-1\), which is impossible. Thus \(s\) is \(1\) or \(2\). The same argument at the right end shows that \(e\) is \(7\) or \(8\).

At either endpoint of the run, the middle cell has one outside horizontal neighbor. Its top and bottom neighbors must both be inside. At every other column of the run, both horizontal neighbors are inside, so exactly one of the top and bottom cells must be inside. Each such interior column therefore gives two independent choices. Any omitted end column is entirely outside.

These choices all produce valid loops. They form a solid middle strip with squares attached above or below it. The strip keeps the region connected and prevents corner-only contacts. Every unchosen top or bottom cell touches the exterior of the grid, and any omitted end column also touches the exterior, so there are no holes. The resulting boundary is one loop that does not intersect itself, and the stated neighbor counts verify every clue.

For \((s,e)=(1,8),(1,7),(2,8),(2,7)\), the run lengths are \(8,7,7,6\). With both endpoint columns fixed, the counts are respectively
\[
2^6,\qquad 2^5,\qquad 2^5,\qquad 2^4.
\]
The cases are disjoint, and different choices give different enclosed cells and hence different toothpick placements. Including the two loops with no enclosed middle cells, the total is
\[
2+64+32+32+16=\boxed{146},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
